projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

address.placeName: 2 Square Robiac, rue de Grenelle, Paris VII

div.p: Mother thanks you very much for your kind letters. She is sorry not to be able to answer you but she is not feeling very well on account of having received bad news a few days ago. Her sister died on in rather unpleasant circumstances in America. Babbo is working pretty hard at present. We are all very glad about our flat which is getting on slowly and will be very nice when all the battering is finished.

closer.salute: Sending Mrs. Pound and yourself our best greetings,

div.note: Nora Joseph Barnacle (1884-1951) had been JJ’s partner since 1904, and formally married him in 1931. They were the parents of Giorgio Joyce (1905-1976) and Lucia Joyce (1907-1982). Lucia had evidently been directed to write this letter by her parents.

Pound had been writing Nora to express good wishes for JJ’s recovery from eye surgery. During 1924-1925, JJ underwent several operations at the hands of Dr. Louis Borsch in Paris. In June 1924, he had a second iridectomy on his left eye (his fifth operation to date); in November 1924, a secondary cataract was removed from his left eye (his sixth operation); and in mid-April 1925, he had a seventh eye operation (Ellmann, JJ 566-70). On 28 April 1925, Pound wrote Nora: “Hope Jim’s operation has been successful and that the matter is now OVER, finished, o.k.” (Robert Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 542).

Nora Barnacle’s younger sister, Annie Barnacle (1889-1925), born in Galway, was one of seven children of Thomas Barnacle (1845-1921) and Honoria or Honoraria “Annie” Healy Barnacle (ca. 1858-1940). Annie had sailed for America in April 1922 and settled in Ogden, Utah, at the home of her sister Mary Josephine (1882-1960), the oldest Barnacle child, who had come to Ogden from Galway in 1906 and married an Englishman, William Henry Blackmore (1882-1939), in 1909 (The Salt Lake Tribune [23 June 1909]: 9). Annie was the twin of Margaret Barnacle (also called Maggie or Peg) (Nora Maddox, Nora: The Real Life of Molly Bloom [Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1988], 229). When Annie emigrated to the United States in 1922, she was 33 years old, but she was listed in the S.S. Baltic’s ship manifest as 24. She maintained this rejuvenating fiction for the rest of her life in America, and was described in her death certificate and obituary as aged 28. Annie had been employed as a checker and laundress at Model Laundry in Ogden. On Friday, 5 June 1925, she enjoyed an evening of music and singing at the home of her sister Mary, joined by their brother Thomas Barnacle (born ca. 1891), who had just arrived from Ireland with the intention of making his home in America. Annie suddenly became ill and within a few hours was dead of a heart attack at 5:30 on Saturday morning, 6 June (The Ogden Standard-Examiner [7 June 1925]: 10). Her death certificate listed “myocarditis” as the cause of death, and “auricular fibrillation” as a contributory cause. The funeral was held at St. Joseph’s Catholic Church in Ogden on the morning of 9 June, with the Reverend William Kennedy reading mass. Annie was buried at Mountain View Cemetery near Ogden (The Ogden Standard-Examiner [9 June 1925]: 6).
It. informal, dad or daddy. JJ’s children, Giorgio and Lucia, grew up speaking Italian, or Triestine Italian, in the household, and continued to speak the language with JJ even when they were older.

JJ had been working at what would eventually be the two concluding chapters of Part I of Finnegans Wake (1939): the Shem chapter, first published in This Quarter (Milan), vol. 1, no. 2 (Autumn-Winter, 1925-1926): 108-23 (FW 169-95), and an early version of the Anna Livia Plurabelle chapter, published in Le Navire d’Argent [Paris], vol. 2, no. 5 (1 October 1925): 59-74 (FW 196-216).

In early June 1925, JJ and family moved from 8 avenue Charles Floquet, near the Eiffel Tower, to a flat about a mile away at 2 Square Robiac, off 192 rue de Grenelle. He remained there “longer than at any other of his Paris addresses, until April 30, 1931” (Ellmann, JJ 571). Stuart Gilbert, who regularly visited JJ, described the flat as a “pleasant apartment in Square Robiac, a by-street in the fashionable ‘Invalides’ district of Paris” (LI 28).

JJ’s Square Robiac apartment had been under repair since he and his family moved in. He wrote Harriet Shaw Weaver on 13 June 1925: “There has been so much hammering and moving going on here that I could scarcely hear my thoughts” (LI 227).
The English artist Dorothy Pound, née Shakespear (1886-1973), who married Pound in London in 1914.
